content: 1. Evidence from non-randomized controlled trials (non-RCTs) suggests that it is uncertain whether multicomponent interventions have any effect on breastfeeding initiation within the first hour after childbirth compared to no intervention or usual care. This is based on very low-certainty evidence. 2. Similarly, it is uncertain whether multicomponent interventions influence exclusive breastfeeding at four months postpartum compared to no intervention or usual care. This conclusion is also based on very low-certainty evidence. 3. There is uncertainty regarding the impact of multicomponent interventions on early initiation of exclusive breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding at one month postpartum, exclusive breastfeeding until six months postpartum, or cessation of exclusive breastfeeding at six months postpartum when compared to no intervention or usual care. All these findings are derived from non-RCTs with very low-certainty evidence. 4. Neonatal morbidity, family care practices, and health service utilization were not reported in the included studies. 5. Regarding intra-household relationship dynamics, it is uncertain whether multicomponent interventions have any effect on father-infant play, caretaking, affection, or attachment at one month postpartum compared to no intervention or usual care. This conclusion is based on non-RCTs with very low-certainty evidence. 6. A qualitative evidence synthesis explored the perceptions of women, men, and health workers regarding interventions aimed at increasing men’s involvement in maternal and newborn health. The findings indicate that men, women, and health workers value access to maternal and newborn health services and high-quality care. This conclusion is supported by high confidence in the evidence. 7. Women, men, and health workers also value the practical and emotional support provided by men to women and newborns. Men, in particular, value opportunities to enhance bonding with their newborns. These findings are supported by high confidence in the evidence. 8. Increased access to and use of maternal and newborn health services, as well as improved care for women and newborns at home associated with greater male engagement, are likely to be valued by women, men, and health workers. Good maternal and newborn health is important to most men, and many are willing to participate in interventions if they believe it will improve health outcomes. This is supported by high confidence in the evidence. 9. No economic evaluations of interventions promoting men’s involvement in maternal and newborn health were identified. However, one study in South Africa assessed the costs of implementing strategies to improve antenatal care services, including couple counseling. The intervention cost nearly 1 million Rand (approximately USD 73,000), with potential for cost reduction in future years. However, the cost per couple counseled would still exceed 300 Rand, requiring further adjustments to improve affordability. 10. Interventions can support improved gender equity in couple or co-parent relationships by empowering men as confident caregivers and encouraging shared responsibility for newborn care. This is supported by moderate confidence in the evidence. 11. Interventions can foster mutual understanding, support, and shared decision-making about maternal and newborn health, contributing to more equitable relationships. This is supported by high confidence in the evidence. 12. Poorly designed or implemented interventions may disproportionately harm single women, women from low-income families, or those in relationships characterized by gender power imbalances. This is supported by moderate confidence in the evidence. 13. Women, men, and families from poorer households may face barriers to accessing the benefits of facility-based interventions involving men, such as men’s presence as labor companions. Economic pressures, insecure work, and lack of parental leave often prevent men from participating. This is supported by low confidence in the evidence. 14. Interventions encouraging partner attendance at antenatal appointments may stigmatize women who attend alone, potentially reducing the quality of care they receive. This is supported by moderate confidence in the evidence. 15. Women in settings with highly unequal gender norms or in relationships with significant power imbalances (e.g., younger women, women in polygamous or violent relationships) are more likely to be negatively affected by poorly designed interventions that reinforce existing inequalities. This is supported by moderate confidence in the evidence. 16. Some men and women may find interventions promoting men’s engagement in maternal and newborn health acceptable if they believe these interventions contribute to better health outcomes or supportive relationships. Conversely, if they believe the interventions increase conflict, they may find them unacceptable. This is supported by low confidence in the evidence. 17. Established gender norms may make messages about men as competent caregivers or shared responsibility for maternal and newborn health unacceptable to some men, women, and health workers. This is supported by low confidence in the evidence. 18. Men are more likely to participate in interventions when they perceive that male involvement in maternal and newborn health is common among their peers. Information, coaching, and encouragement through interventions can increase men’s confidence to engage further. 19. Interventions promoting men’s participation in facility-based maternal and newborn health services are more feasible in settings with enabling health system environments. This is supported by high confidence in the evidence. 20. In lowand middle-income countries, limited health system capacity to make services more male-friendly (e.g., through training, service delivery changes, or physical space modifications) may discourage men’s participation. Established gender norms that discourage male involvement also act as barriers. This is supported by low confidence in the evidence. 21. Tailoring interventions to accommodate men’s availability, such as adjusting timing and location, may increase participation. This is supported by low confidence in the evidence. 22. The use of home-based records, as a complement to facility-based records, is recommended for the care of pregnant and postpartum women, newborns, and children. These records can improve care-seeking behavior, men’s involvement and support, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and communication between health workers and caregivers. 23. Home-based records, such as vaccination cards or child health books, are health documents kept in the household to record an individual’s health service history. They are intended to complement facility-based records and integrate into health information systems. 24. Digital targeted client communication is recommended for behavior change in sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health, provided concerns about sensitive content and data privacy are addressed. This intervention can improve health behaviors and reduce inequities among individuals with access to mobile devices. 25. Digital birth notifications are recommended in settings where they provide individual-level data to health or civil registration systems, and where these systems have the capacity to respond to the notifications.
